# High-Performance LLM Inference: A Technical Deep Dive into Continuous Batching, KV Caches, and Advanced Decoding Strategies

The deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) in production environments presents a unique set of engineering challenges that differ significantly from traditional machine learning inference tasks. Unlike classification or regression models, which typically process fixed-size inputs and produce fixed-size outputs in a single forward pass, LLMs are autoregressive. They generate text token-by-token, where each new token depends on the entire sequence of previously generated tokens. This sequential dependency creates a fundamental tension between latency (the time it takes to generate the first token and subsequent tokens) and throughput (the number of tokens or requests processed per second). To resolve this tension, modern LLM inference servers have evolved sophisticated mechanisms including continuous batching, Key-Value (KV) caching, prefix reuse, and speculative decoding. This tutorial provides a detailed technical analysis of these mechanisms, explaining how they interact to optimize performance in high-concurrency environments.

## 1. The Fundamental Bottleneck: Memory Bandwidth vs. Compute

To understand why these optimizations are necessary, one must first understand the hardware bottleneck of LLM inference. Modern GPUs are designed for massive parallelism, offering immense floating-point operations per second (FLOPS). However, LLM inference, particularly during the generation phase, is often memory-bound rather than compute-bound.

In a transformer model, the attention mechanism requires accessing the Key and Value tensors for all previous tokens in the sequence. As the sequence length grows, the amount of data that must be read from High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) to the on-chip SRAM increases linearly. Meanwhile, the actual computation (matrix multiplications) for generating a single token is relatively small compared to the data movement required to fetch the model weights and the KV cache. This phenomenon is known as the "memory wall." If an inference server processes requests one by one (static batching), the GPU sits idle waiting for memory transfers, resulting in extremely low utilization. The primary goal of all subsequent optimizations is to maximize the arithmetic intensity of the workload, ensuring that the GPU spends more time computing and less time waiting for data.

They generate text token by token, where each new token depends on the entire history of previously generated tokens. During the "prefill" phase, the model processes the entire input prompt in parallel, computing the attention scores for all tokens simultaneously. This phase is compute-bound, meaning it is limited by the speed of the GPU’s floating-point operations (FLOPS).

However, during the "decode" phase, the model generates one token at a time. For each new token, the model must attend to all previous tokens in the sequence. Furthermore, because the generation of token $t$ depends on token $t-1$, we cannot parallelize the generation of multiple tokens for a single request. This sequential nature means that if we process requests one by one, the GPU remains idle for significant portions of the time, waiting for the next token to be generated.
